item.title: Geometric ergodicity of Gibbs samplers for linear mixed models with several heavy-tailed random-effect components and unknown tail parameters
item.description: arXiv:2611.28413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear mixed models with heavy-tailed random effects are widely used for robust Bayesian analysis of longitudinal data. We study the three-block Gibbs sampler for such models when the random effects are split into several components, such as random intercepts and slopes, each with its own scale and its own scale mixture of normals, when the tail parameters have priors on finite grids and are drawn jointly with the latent weights, and when the random-effects design is rank deficient, as when some subjects contribute a single observation. We give sufficient conditions for geometric ergodicity that attribute the rank deficiency to the components that cause it, and show that, under conditions on the gamma priors on the precision parameters, they hold for Student-t and slash random effects with individual weights, any grid of tail parameters and any design. The result extends to random-effect vectors whose coordinates share a weight, for subject-specific designs with known shape matrices. It justifies Monte Carlo standard errors for regression coefficients, log-scales and posterior probabilities of the tail parameters. Simulations show that the scale and the tail parameter can mix much more slowly than the regression coefficients, and an analysis of beta-HCG data illustrates the methods.
item.dc:creator: Rolando de la Cruz, Nathalie Humeniy

item.title: KernelMix: Bayesian kernel machine regression in Python
item.description: arXiv:2611.28634v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exposures measured together can have nonlinear associations with an outcome, and the association with one exposure may depend on another. Bayesian kernel machine regression represents these patterns through a flexible exposure-response function. We implement this approach in KernelMix, a Python package. To handle different outcome types, KernelMix combines the exposure function with continuous, binary, count and survival models, including selected extensions for clustered observations and censored event times. For fitted models, it returns posterior summaries, uncertainty intervals, joint predictions and sampling diagnostics. Fitting and prediction use NumPy and SciPy without requiring R. To assess the implementation, we compare selected Gaussian and probit posterior summaries and conditional calculations with installed R bkmr 0.2.2 and check additional model components against independent mathematical calculations. A daily ozone analysis illustrates how these components form an analysis workflow.
item.dc:creator: Nilson Chapagain

item.title: Fast likelihood evaluation for multivariate sensory discrimination models
item.description: arXiv:2611.28865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sensory discrimination is often measured by fitting statistical models with likelihood functions that are computationally challenging to evaluate. In the standard triangle and duo-trio tests, a subject is presented with three stimuli, two of one kind and one of another, and is asked to identify the odd one out (the triangle test) or which of two stimuli matches a reference (the duo-trio test). In a Thurstonian model, the subject's internal representation of each stimulus is a Gaussian whose mean and covariance depend on the stimulus, and the probability that the subject's response is correct is an integral over a $3d$-dimensional Gaussian with no closed form for $d > 1$, where $d$ is the dimension of the stimulus space. To fit a statistical model to data collected from triangle or duo-trio tests, the likelihood function, and often its gradient, need to be evaluated many times, making statistical inference inefficient. Here, we introduce fast algorithms for evaluating certain classes of likelihood functions for the triangle and duo-trio tests. The algorithms rely on reducing the dimension of these functions. The triangle probability, a function of $2d + d(d+1)$ arguments, reduces analytically to a function of $2d$ arguments, and the duo-trio probability, when the two stimuli have equal covariances, reduces to a function of a single scalar for any $d$. After reducing the dimensionality of those functions, we use neural networks and Chebyshev expansions to evaluate the lower-dimensional functions efficiently. Our algorithms demonstrate orders of magnitude speedups over existing approaches at comparable accuracy, both for a single evaluation and when used to compute the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of a model of color discrimination. The dimensionality reduction we use generalizes to non-Gaussian noise models with elliptical level sets, and to tests with more than three stimuli.
item.dc:creator: Philip Greengard, Fangfang Hong, David H. Brainard, Alex Williams

item.title: Kemeny median rankings with ties under constraints on the buckets
item.description: arXiv:2611.28925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The median ranking is the ranking that minimizes the sum of the Kemeny distances from the rankings expressed by a set of judges. In many applications the consensus requires a prescribed structure: a given number of buckets, given sizes of all or some of the buckets, as in the forced distributions of Q methodology, or the form of a top-$k$ list. We show that all these problems are a single problem, the search for the median ranking among the rankings whose pattern of bucket sizes is admissible, and that they depend on the data only through the combined input matrix, defined by Emond and Mason in 2002. On this matrix we build BOLT, a deterministic heuristic that combines a set of starting solutions, a local search that moves one object at a time and can create or remove ties, and the exact best partition of a fixed order of the objects into buckets with an admissible pattern. We also provide an exact solution for the median top-$k$ list. The solutions of BOLT are assessed, on real and simulated data, against the optimum certified by a binary linear programming formulation, adapted to the Kemeny distance and to the constraints on the buckets, and against the methods available in the literature. Applications to Q-sorts, top-$k$ lists and large and sparse data sets of ratings show how the constrained problems arise in practice, and how the treatment of the objects not ranked by the judges changes the solution.
item.dc:creator: Maurizio Romano, Luca Coraggio, Claudio Conversano, Antonio D'Ambrosio

item.title: Exact, narrow and fast: Use the Gaffke confidence interval for the mean of a discrete bounded variable
item.description: arXiv:2611.29512v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Survey ratings, test scores and many other data take a few known values, and we often want a confidence interval for their mean. For small samples, or for means close to the smallest or largest value, the usual intervals cover the true mean much less often than they claim. The interval of Gaffke generalizes the Clopper-Pearson interval to any finite set of values, and a recent proof of Gaffke's conjecture shows that its coverage is at least the nominal level for every sample size and every distribution. Its endpoints, however, are quantiles of a weighted sum of Dirichlet variables, with no closed form. This note makes three contributions. First, a fast and accurate algorithm for the endpoints: a Fourier inversion integral on a line through the saddle point gives tail probabilities with a small relative error, a Gauss-Legendre rule on geometric panels converges at the same rate wherever the singularities are, and a Newton iteration needs 2.6 evaluations per endpoint on average. The cost is $O(kN)$ operations for $k$ values and $N$ quadrature nodes, and $N$ does not grow with the sample size, so an interval takes less than a millisecond for any $n$. Second, an experimental comparison with the published intervals: for $n \le 30$, the Gaffke interval is the shortest of the intervals that keep the level, 17 to 20% shorter than the betting interval of Waudby-Smith and Ramdas and 19 to 37% shorter than Anderson's, while the shorter intervals (Wald, Student, profile likelihood, Bayesian) cover the mean less than 50% of the time for some distributions. Third, tested Python and R packages and a web page, with endpoints accurate to $10^{-12}$ of the range of the values. So the interval is exact, narrow and fast, and we recommend it.
item.dc:creator: Louis Abraham

item.title: Computational Strategies for Mixed Logit Estimation Automatic Differentiation, GPU Computing, and Floating-Point Precision
item.description: arXiv:2611.29833v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixed logit estimation can become computationally demanding as sample size and the dimension of preference heterogeneity increase. This study examines how derivative computation, processor choice and floating-point precision affect estimation time and parameter recovery across problem sizes. This paper provides a controlled benchmark, comparing finite differences (FD) with automatic differentiation (AD), central processing unit (CPU) execution with graphics processing unit (GPU) execution, and double-precision (FP64) with single-precision (FP32) arithmetic using Monte Carlo experiments that hold the data-generating process, simulation draws, optimiser, starting values, and objective function fixed across strategies. The results show that AD is the dominant source of acceleration. Combining AD with FP32 arithmetic provides further gains, while combining AD, GPU execution, and FP32 arithmetic delivers the largest speed improvements, particularly as sample size and model complexity increase. Our findings indicate substantial computational gains with broadly comparable parameter-recovery performance in the simulated settings considered.An empirical application in health preferences illustrates what extra empirical evidence and statistical benefit on model fit could be achieved, when researchers are made possible to estimate a richer, correlated preference specification. We provide an open sourced prototype to for model estimation with AD-FP32 strategy workflow that automatically detect hardware and provide the fastest estimation. Faster estimation can make richer random-coefficient specifications, larger simulation draw counts, bootstrap inference, multi-start optimisation, and robustness checks more feasible in applied choice modelling research.
item.dc:creator: Hengzhe Zhao Jinhui Zhang Yuanyuan Gu

item.title: StatClaim: Study Designs as Types, Protocols as Programs and Statistical Claims as Proof Obligations
item.description: arXiv:2611.30021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Statistical guarantees depend on the compatibility of a study's model, hypotheses, sampling plan and analysis. StatClaim is a declarative domain-specific language for encoding research protocols and statistical analysis plans as programs built from objects whose types encode their statistical roles within the study design. The compiler checks type compatibility and applies contracts to check additional requirements on the values and relationships of these objects. When verification is requested, StatClaim's backend constructs and checks proofs of supported statistical claims using Lean under stated assumptions. These claims concern Type I error, familywise error, power and interval coverage, including supported combinations of analyses and procedures with planned stopping rules. Reports distinguish formally proved, conditional, cited and author-declared guarantees and provide replayable certificates for verified claims. The same specification supports sample-size searches, power calculations and interval-precision assessment using exact calculations, analytical approximations or reproducible simulation. A command-line interface, editor integration and graphical block editor use a shared compiler and execution layer. Validation reproduces 102 optimal and minimax two-stage designs from Simon's published tables and verifies their error and power bounds in Lean. A clinical trial case study illustrates partial encoding of a published analysis plan using cited methods and conditional proofs. The open-source implementation includes runnable tutorials and examples for specifying and checking study designs before outcomes are collected.
item.dc:creator: Supun Manathunga

item.title: Neural Schr\"{o}dinger Bridge via Yasue Action with Applications to Generative Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.28623v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a novel neural solver for inferring the continuous state evolution of the Schr\"{o}dinger bridge problem. The proposed solver builds on a saddle point formulation involving the Yasue action functional. This allows us to realize the continuous state evolution by learning the optimal velocity for an ordinary differential equation, as opposed to learning the optimal drift for a stochastic differential equation. The proposed solver only uses the source and the target samples, and not the source and target distributions per se, which makes it particularly suitable for high dimensional applications arising in generative modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solver using several numerical experiments in low and high dimensions, using both real and synthetic datasets.
item.dc:creator: Yan-Han Chen, Abhishek Halder, Hailiang Liu

item.title: Community Detection in Fuzzy Social Networks through Fuzzy Co-Membership Relations over Alpha-Cut Realizations
item.description: arXiv:2611.29342v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In fuzzy social networks the ties between actors are triangular fuzzy numbers, and community detection applied to their cores ignores how the partition depends on their vagueness. We propose a fuzzy co-membership relation obtained by running the Louvain algorithm on crisp networks compatible with the alpha-cuts of the ties and integrating the proportions of co-assignment over alpha. The relation is positive semidefinite; from it we derive a consensus partition, the number of groups, membership degrees and an assignment ambiguity index. In simulations from stochastic block models the relation does not yield better partitions than symmetric perturbations of the cores of the same size. Its ambiguity index is more closely associated with the structural position of the actors and identifies actors split between two groups when the vagueness is concentrated on them; when the asymmetry of the fuzzy ties points towards the latent tie strength, its co-membership degrees have a lower Brier score. The interval-weighted Louvain algorithm estimates the number of communities more accurately. In two departmental collaboration networks the observed ambiguity is lower than under permuted ratings, while the partitions depend on the symmetrization of directed ratings and on the coding of non-response.
item.dc:creator: Annamaria Porreca, Fabrizio Maturo

item.title: Quantitative Convergence of Hit-and-Run Beyond Log-Concavity via Variational Hypocoercivity
item.description: arXiv:2611.30691v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the convergence to equilibrium of Hit-and-Run, a popular generalisation of the Gibbs sampler. To this end, we establish a novel connection between Hit-and-Run and the theory of variational hypocoercivity, an approach to establish convergence of continuous-time Markov processes. To bridge the gap between the discrete-time Hit-and-Run chain and hypocoercivity, we introduce Hit-and-Langevin, a continuous-time Markov process that approximates Hit-and-Run in an appropriate sense. Using the second-order lift and flow Poincar\'e inequality formulation of variational hypocoercivity, we show convergence of Hit-and-Langevin and deduce a lower bound on the spectral gap of Hit-and-Run. Notably, our analysis seamlessly extends beyond the extensively studied setting of log-concave target distributions, marking the first substantial departure from this setting beyond quasi-log-concave and uniform distributions. More broadly, this work demonstrates that discrete, non-local dynamics, such as Hit-and-Run, can be made amenable to powerful analytical methods, such as variational hypocoercivity.
item.dc:creator: Francis L\"orler, Stefan Oberd\"orster

item.title: Fast and Consistent Structure Learning in Graphical Models via Approximate Cross-Validation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30822v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Structure learning for sparse graphical models in high dimensions requires both computational scalability and selection consistency. Classical criteria such as (Extended) Bayesian Information Criterion can provide consistency, but rely on model-specific likelihoods and complexity calibration. In comparison, cross-validation avoids such analytic calibration and is therefore attractive for graph learning. However, cross-validation is computationally infeasible and theoretically inconsistent in structure learning. This creates a tension between consistency and flexibility in modeling. In this work, we resolve the tension by developing a scalable graph-recovery procedure built on approximate cross-validation. We demonstrate its effectiveness in learning large graphical models both theoretically and empirically, and establish selection consistency under mild signal strength assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Lyu, Mladen Kolar, Bryon Aragam

item.title: Spurious Information in Large Markets: Random Matrix Laws for Entropy, Mutual Information and the Value of Information
item.description: arXiv:2611.30998v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Entropy, Kullback-Leibler divergence and mutual information have become standard currencies for measuring how much one set of financial variables reveals about another. In large cross-sections they are almost always computed from sample covariance matrices, and the noise in those matrices is the object of random matrix theory. This paper develops the random matrix theory of Gaussian information functionals and applies it to markets. I show that the plug-in mutual information between two blocks of p and r variables estimated from $n$ observations has an exact expected excess, the spurious information, that is a digamma telescope independent of the true dependence. Under independence its law is that of a product of Beta variables. In the proportional regime it grows linearly with an order-one variance. The same quantity is a linear spectral statistic of the Jacobi ensemble, which yields a closed form for the logarithmic moment of Wachter's law. Spurious information increases strictly whenever uninformative coordinates are added. In a CARA-Gaussian economy the certainty-equivalent value of a signal equals mutual information divided by risk aversion, so these results translate one for one into a spurious value of information. The canonical-correlation phase transition then defines a frontier of minimum detectable information. On daily returns of 49 US industry portfolios from 1990 to 2026, I document the market mode, the reliability of sector eigenvectors implied by the BBP transition, the out-of-sample cost of noise dressing, and an information linkage between carbon-intensive and financial industries that survives exact bias correction and conditioning on the market.
item.dc:creator: James Rice

item.title: Automated Techniques for Efficient Sampling of Piecewise-Deterministic Markov Processes
item.description: arXiv:2408.03682v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) are a class of continuous-time Markov processes that have recently been used to develop a new class of Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms. However, implementing these processes is challenging because of their continuous-time nature and the need to integrate the rate function. Recently, Corbella, Spencer, and Roberts (2022) proposed a new algorithm that automates the implementation of the Zig-Zag sampler. However, the efficiency of the algorithm depends strongly on a hyperparameter ($t_{\mathrm{max}}$) that remains fixed throughout the run and must be tuned through preliminary runs. In this work, we relax this constraint and propose a new variant of the algorithm that allows this parameter to change over time and adapt automatically to the target distribution. We also replace Brent's optimization algorithm with a grid-based method for computing an upper bound on the rate function. This method is more robust to irregularities in the function and produces a tighter upper bound more quickly. We also extend the algorithm to other PDMPs and provide a Python implementation based on JAX.
item.dc:creator: Charly Andral, Kengo Kamatani

item.title: Coresets for Density-Based Clustering via Bayesian Predictive Partition Matching
item.description: arXiv:2502.05725v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Density-based clustering identifies groups as connected high-density regions, accommodating irregular shapes and reflecting their geometry, but this reliance on density estimation introduces uncertainty into the resulting partitions, which is often costly to quantify. To represent this uncertainty efficiently, we construct a compact representation of the data, or coreset, designed to preserve the distribution of predictive density-based partitions. We sample observations from a Dirichlet process surrogate, smooth them to estimate densities, and use the resulting level sets to partition a common reference set. Starting from a uniform subsample, we learn an affine transformation that improves agreement with full-data partitions by minimizing a tractable approximation to paired expected variation of information. Fresh, independent predictive simulations then guide the selection of the final transformation. Our analysis provides approximation and selection guarantees and establishes consistency for ideal fixed-resolution partitions under geometric conditions. Simulations and an application to mass cytometry show improved partition agreement over uniform subsampling, often matching substantially larger supports.
item.dc:creator: Bernardo Flores

item.title: Rate-Optimal Randomised Kernel Quadrature
item.description: arXiv:2605.18134v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Kernel quadrature is used to approximate integrals of smooth functions, with the worst-case error typically decaying at the minimax rate $n^{-\alpha/d}$ for smoothness $\alpha$ in dimension $d$. Existing rate-optimal methods often depend on deterministic point sets, sometimes tailored to a specific kernel. Here, we study randomised designs for kernel quadrature on compact and unbounded domains for kernels whose reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces are norm-equivalent to Sobolev spaces of integer order $\alpha>d/2$. We bound the worst-case error of prescribed designs adapted to a sampling density $p$ by $n^{-\alpha/d}$ times an explicit functional of the sampling and integration densities. Minimising this factor gives $p^\star\propto\pi^\gamma$ with $\gamma=2d/(2\alpha+d)$, where $\pi$ is the integration density. The proposal depends on the kernel only through its Sobolev order $\alpha$. Under local mass and cell-average conditions, together with a tail condition on $\mathbb{R}^d$, independent samples from $p^\star$ attain the same minimax rate with high probability, up to a logarithmic factor. The same bound also controls posterior contraction. We verify these conditions for Beta-type densities on the cube and, for integrands in $\mathcal{H}^\alpha(\mathbb{R}^d)$, for Gaussian and Student-$t$ measures. The deterministic minimax exponent for Student targets is $\min(\alpha,\nu+d/2)/d$, with a logarithmic gap between the bounds at $\alpha=\nu+d/2$.
item.dc:creator: Edoardo Bandoni (CEREMADE), Christian Robert (CEREMADE), Julien Stoehr (CEREMADE)

item.title: A Two Stage Quasi-Likelihood Estimation Method for High Dimensional Generalized Structural Equation Models
item.description: arXiv:2608.16017v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Estimating high dimensional Generalized Structural Equation Models presents severe computational challenges. Traditional simultaneous estimators frequently suffer from numerical instability and prohibitive computational costs. Moreover, there are no tractable algorithms for families such as Poisson, negative binomial, and gamma. To overcome these limitations, this article introduces a Two Stage Quasi-Likelihood Expectation-Maximization framework. The proposed method isolates the structural model from the measurement model. First, it approximates the conditional distribution of the latent variables given the observed indicators. Second, it employs marginal quasi-likelihood estimating equations to evaluate the structural parameters, deriving the necessary conditional moments either exactly or through Monte Carlo integration. This approach completely avoids the need to evaluate the full joint likelihood. Extensive simulations demonstrate that our method drastically reduces computational runtime, providing a numerically stable framework that minimizes the mean squared error and structural bias to yield a scalable and flexible solution for analyzing complex latent variable models.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad W. Hattab

item.title: Does Increasing Government Spending on Tertiary Education Provide a Return on Investment? A Bayesian Causal Inference Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.18086v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Does public spending on tertiary (university) education generate a positive fiscal return once general economic growth is separated out? Cross-country data make this hard to answer because growing economies naturally collect more tax, international ratios divide per-student spending by GDP per person and student headcount, and cohorts take years to graduate. We assemble a five-year panel of 121 countries (1985-2024) and fit continuous-treatment Multivariate Bayesian Causal Forests modelling four tax changes jointly whilst adjusting for starting conditions, predicted funding, and follow-up growth. A +10 percentage-point (pp) increase in per-student spending (% of GDP per person) shifts the tax mix toward direct income and profit taxation by +0.36 pp after 5 years (P = 0.93, posterior probability of a positive effect) and +0.71 pp after 10 years (P = 0.96). Overall tax-to-GDP takes a decade to respond: 10-year total non-resource tax rises by +0.24 pp of GDP (P = 0.89; +0.31 pp, P = 0.94 across four chains, retaining the conservative single-chain baseline) and direct income tax by +0.12 pp (P = 0.90; +0.15 pp, P = 0.93 across four chains) per +10 pp of per-student spending, by +0.37 pp (P > 0.99) after five-year within-country increases, and by +0.22 pp in total tax (P = 0.95) and +0.15 pp in direct income tax (P = 0.98) per +25% increase in real PPP dollars per student. Comparing one cohort's degree cost against its 40-year career taxes shows a typical three- to five-fold expected total tax return in high-income economies with wide intervals reflecting macro noise (EUR 2.4B in Ireland returning EUR 9.7B in total tax, 95% CI EUR -10B to +32B, net-profit probability 0.77, and EUR 2.9B in direct income tax; EUR 11.6B in the UK returning EUR 58B, 95% CI EUR -60B to +190B), whereas expanding the budget without protecting spending per student yields no return.
item.dc:creator: Andrew C. Parnell
